Triggers.value: When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is hard to reconcile with this patient's demographics (22-year-old single male auditor) and the rest of the profile unless there is a specific unreported context such as concealment or gender expression. In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette: Two years ago, Samir sat in a colleague’s apartment reviewing a shared ledger after hours. The air hung heavy with clove smoke and a thick, synthetic cologne. A man he had been messaging with for weeks shifted his tone, ignoring Samir’s repeated protests and dismissing his boundaries with a casual, dismissive laugh. When the man pinned him down, he muttered something about how “my ex never argued,” treating Samir’s distress as an inconvenience. Samir froze, certain that a different man would have escaped the situation, that he was simply careless or weak. What settled over him afterward was a profound humiliation, a shame that clung to him like the lingering, sweet smoke. In the months that followed, the memory of that room unfolded into his daily life. A whiff of matching cologne on a subway platform made his chest tighten and his breath catch. He found himself watching crowds, his attention fixed on people who disregarded basic courtesy or blatantly violated social boundaries, the sight of it sparking a familiar, cold dread. When acquaintances recounted stories using phrases like “my ex always,” his stomach dropped, the words unlocking a visceral panic he could not articulate. He began wearing long-sleeved jackets and oversized coats well past spring, pulling the fabric close to himself. He told himself it was merely practical, but in truth, he was trying to make himself smaller, to avoid drawing attention. Samir works as an auditor, spending his days scanning financial records and rotating through client offices. The routine that once felt orderly now felt unpredictable. He mapped every floor plan the moment he crossed the threshold, his eyes constantly tracking fire escapes and service corridors. He refused seating in the center of conference rooms, insisting on positions near the door, convinced that an open layout offered no way out. When a junior associate leaned abruptly over his desk to highlight a discrepancy, the sudden movement made Samir’s shoulders snap tight, his breath hitching in a throat that had been braced for impact since that night. His muscles remained perpetually wound, waiting for the next threat to surface. He stopped entering unfamiliar client buildings, convinced that without a clear assessment of the exits and the layout, he would be trapped. The reluctance to sit in situations where his appearance or performance might be scrutinized developed alongside the rest of his withdrawal. Client meetings felt like interrogations, and he began declining invitations to firm reviews, citing scheduling conflicts. The professional consequence appeared quietly but steadily. He missed a critical review at a downtown financial district tower, unable to navigate the glass elevator lobby or trust the acoustics of the unfamiliar stairwells. A senior partner noted his consistent withdrawals during team evaluations, leaving Samir feeling exposed and judged. He replayed the assault repeatedly, comparing himself to colleagues who navigated the same streets and offices without fear. The man he used to be—eager, light-hearted, unafraid to take up space—was gone, replaced by a quiet, grinding misery that colored every morning. At twenty-two, Samir sits in a clinic waiting room, his coat sleeves pulled over his hands, his eyes tracking the door. His supervisor finally insisted he seek support, citing his slipping work quality and the growing distance from his team. He is terrified that speaking openly will confirm what he already believes: that he is fundamentally damaged, that the humiliation is permanent, that he will never reclaim the happiness he once carried. What he hopes for, quietly, is a way to walk into a room and simply breathe, to let his shoulders drop, and to stop bracing for the sound of his own name.
